name: Key Contract Terms for Room Additions in Los Angeles County

mainEntity.name: What should be in a Los Angeles County room addition contract to protect me from change-order surprises and city inspection delays?
mainEntity.text: What should be in a Los Angeles County room addition contract to protect me from change-order surprises and city inspection delays?

acceptedAnswer.text: For a room addition in Los Angeles County, your contract is your main protection against cost overruns and delays. It should start with a detailed scope of work referencing specific plans, structural details, and finish schedules, not just a one-page description. Require line-item pricing for major trades so you can understand where costs might change. Include clear allowances for items like fixtures, tile, and flooring, plus written rules for what happens if you exceed those allowances. Insist that any change to the scope, materials, or layout must be documented as a signed change order showing added cost and extra time before work proceeds. Spell out who is responsible for obtaining permits, scheduling inspections, and responding to city plan-check comments. Your contract should clarify whether you or the contractor pay for plan revisions and any extra engineering required by the city. Add language explaining how inspection delays, red tags, or required corrections affect the schedule and potential added costs. Use a milestone-based payment schedule tied to completed work stages (e.g., foundation, framing, rough-in, drywall) rather than large upfront payments. Confirm that the contract lists license number, insurance details, warranty terms, and how disputes are handled. Walking through these details before you sign reduces surprises once construction starts.
acceptedAnswer.description: A solid Los Angeles County room addition contract should clearly define scope of work, detailed plans, allowances, change-order rules, payment schedule, permit responsibilities, and handling of inspection delays. Require written change orders, caps on allowances, timelines tied to milestones, and clarity on who pays for revisions due to city comments.
